demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: For trauma involving unexpected death of a loved one, repeated triggers centered on children (kids crying, being around children) are hard to explain unless the deceased was a child or the death specifically involved children; with no supporting memory, threat, or appraisal content linking the loss to children, this trigger pattern is clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: Avoiding sex is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The reported triggers and appraisals focus on grief/disconnection rather than bodily violation, intimacy threat, or sexual trauma themes, so this strategy appears to address a symptom domain absent elsewhere in the selected items.

Feeling 'like an object, not like a person' is more characteristic of interpersonal violation, coercion, or depersonalized trauma responses. In a bereavement profile, without corroborating memory, trigger, or strategy content suggesting objectification or dissociation, this appraisal is difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For traumatic bereavement, 'being around children' is not impossible as a trigger, but in this profile it lacks support from the other selected items. There are no memory, threat, or appraisal items linking the loss to children or parenting, so this trigger feels clinically unanchored relative to the rest of the profile.

'Avoid Sex' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the self-report. Sexual avoidance is more typically anchored to interpersonal/sexual trauma or marked contamination/intimacy themes, none of which are represented elsewhere in the selected triggers or appraisals for a bereavement presentation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person
issues.explanation: 'I feel like an object, not like a person' is poorly matched to unexpected death of a loved one in the absence of other humiliation, assault, or depersonalization-related content. It does not cohere well with the grief-linked triggers and appears disconnected from the stated maladaptive strategies and formulation.

vignette:
# Rosa's Story

Rosa Delgado was forty-two when she found her younger brother Miguel collapsed on the kitchen floor of their shared apartment. She had come home from her shift at the automotive parts factory expecting to make dinner; instead, she found him unresponsive, his body already cooling. The paramedics arrived within minutes—she heard the sirens wailing up the street, that high-pitched wail that seemed to split the air itself—but Miguel was already gone. The doctors said it was a sudden cardiac event, something no one had seen coming. He was only thirty-four.

In the weeks that followed, Rosa moved through the funeral arrangements in a fog. She selected his casket, chose flowers, sat in the front pew of the church while people filed past to offer their condolences. Her sister flew in from Phoenix; her mother wept inconsolably. Rosa felt nothing at first, only a vast emptiness where her brother should have been. Miguel had been her closest confidant, the person who made her laugh, who knew her completely. They had grown up together in the apartment, had navigated their parents' divorce side by side, had become each other's anchor in a chaotic childhood. Now he was simply gone.

The first few months were the worst. Every siren—whether an ambulance passing the factory or a fire truck racing down her street—sent Rosa into a spiral of panic and dread. The sound would trigger an immediate, visceral memory of that day, and she would find herself replaying the moment she discovered him over and over, searching for something she might have missed, some detail that could rewrite what had happened. If only she had come home ten minutes earlier. If only she had insisted he see a doctor about his occasional chest tightness. She would lie awake at night, reconstructing conversations, analyzing his final words to her the night before, convinced that somewhere in the sequence of events lay proof that she could have prevented this. This obsessive review consumed hours—she would sit at her kitchen table, the same table where she used to eat breakfast with Miguel, going through every interaction from the weeks before his death, as if understanding exactly how and why it happened would somehow make it bearable, or even reversible.

When her coworker Javier mentioned that his father had passed away, Rosa felt her chest tighten. The mention of loss—the casual way he spoke about his grief—triggered an immediate sense of dread and a desperate need for reassurance. She found herself asking Javier repeatedly whether she seemed okay, whether he thought she was handling things well, whether she seemed like she was falling apart. His confused but kind reassurances never lasted long; within hours, the anxiety would creep back, and she would text her sister asking the same questions again. She had come to believe that she no longer belonged anywhere, that the death of the person closest to her had fundamentally severed her from normal life. The happiness she used to feel—the lightness that once defined her—seemed like something from another person's life entirely. Her life had been destroyed by this loss, and no amount of reassurance could convince her otherwise.

The avoidance began almost without her noticing. When her church announced a memorial service for parishioners who had passed that year, Rosa called in sick to work. The thought of sitting in a cemetery, of being surrounded by grief and graves, felt unbearable. She stopped attending family dinners when she knew her mother would want to talk about Miguel, stopped visiting the apartment's kitchen when possible, started taking longer routes home from the factory to avoid driving past the hospital where he had been pronounced dead. Each time she avoided something—a funeral, a conversation about loss, a place that held a memory—the relief was immediate but short-lived. The avoidance seemed to prove to her that the world was genuinely dangerous, that grief was contagious, that she was right to isolate herself. And the more she withdrew, the more convinced she became that she truly did not belong anywhere, that her life would never be whole again. By the time she sought help, Rosa was spending most evenings alone in her apartment, unable to listen to the radio without scanning for sirens, unable to answer a phone call without fearing bad news, unable to imagine a future in which she was anything other than the woman her brother's death had broken.
